stimulus.text: Although Eastern North Pacific (ENP) gray whales generally migrate between their wintering waters along the coast of Mexico and their foraging waters in the Arctic, a subset of this population — known as the Pacific Coast Feeding Group (PCFG) — forages along the coastlines of Northern California (USA) and British Columbia (Canada) instead. Interestingly, individuals in this subset reach smaller maximum sizes than other ENP whales do, despite having similar pre-maximum growth rates. Researchers hypothesize that this difference may be an adaptation to distinct resource opportunities in the PCFG foraging range.

stem.text: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers’ claim regarding the size of PCFG whales?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The average body size of PCFG whales observed along the coasts of Northern California and British Columbia has remained relatively steady in recent decades, while the average body size of ENP whales in the main group has slightly decreased.

choices.label: B
choices.text: When present along the coasts of Northern California and British Columbia, PCFG whales tend to forage in rocky kelp beds at shallow depths inaccessible to whales as large as those in the ENP main group.

choices.label: C
choices.text: When foraging along the coasts of Northern California and British Columbia, PCFG whales are in closer proximity to major ports and urban populations than ENP whales in the main group are when foraging in Arctic waters.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Certain crustacean prey species available along the coasts of Northern California and British Columbia where PCFG whales tend to forage are not available in the Arctic waters where ENP whales in the main group forage.

explanation.text:
Choice B is the best answer because it presents a finding that, if true, would most directly support the researchers’ hypothesis that the smaller maximum size of PCFG whales is an adaptation to resource opportunities particular to their foraging range. The text explains that PCFG whales, a subgroup of ENP gray whales, forage along the coasts of Northern California and British Columbia rather than in the Arctic, where the main ENP group forages. The text goes on to state that PCFG whales reach smaller maximum sizes than other ENP gray whales despite having similar pre-maximum growth rates. If PCFG whales tend to forage in shallow, rocky kelp beds that whales as large as those in the main group cannot access, that would indicate that smaller body size confers a direct advantage in this foraging range — namely, access to a food source that larger whales cannot reach.

Choice A is incorrect because a finding describing recent trends in average body size for both groups of whales wouldn’t address whether the smaller maximum size of PCFG whales reflects an adaptation to their foraging environment. Recent stability or change in average size doesn’t speak to why the size difference between PCFG whales and the main ENP group exists. Choice C is incorrect because a finding about PCFG whales’ proximity to ports and urban populations wouldn’t address the resources available to PCFG whales or the relationship between body size and foraging. Proximity to human activity is irrelevant to a hypothesis about body size being an adaptation to resource opportunities. Choice D is incorrect. Although a finding about a certain prey species being available in the PCFG whales’ foraging waters but not in the main group of ENP whales’ foraging waters would establish that the PCFG foraging range offers distinct prey species, it wouldn’t connect the availability of those prey species to body size in a way that would explain the PCFG whales’ smaller size. Without indicating that the available prey in the PCFG range favors smaller whales, the finding falls short of supporting the hypothesis that smaller size is an adaptation to resource opportunities.

stem.text: Botanists recognize over fifty different species of sunflower. One species, the silverleaf sunflower, ______ both an early-flowering ecotype that tends to grow in coastal areas and a late-flowering ecotype that grows inland. Choice A is incorrect. This doesn’t complete the text in a way that conforms to the conventions of Standard English. This verb needs to function as the main verb in the sentence, with the subject “one species,” so it needs to be conjugated. “Having included” is a participle form of the verb: it’s not conjugated and doesn’t function like a normal verb. Choice B is incorrect. This doesn’t complete the text in a way that conforms to the conventions of Standard English. This verb needs to function as the main verb in the sentence, with the subject “one species,” so it needs to be conjugated. “Including” is the gerund form of the verb: it’s not conjugated and doesn’t function like a normal verb. Choice C is incorrect. This doesn’t complete the text in a way that conforms to the conventions of Standard English. This verb needs to function as the main verb in the sentence, with the subject “one species,” so it needs to be conjugated. “To include” is the infinitive form of the verb: it’s not conjugated.

stimulus.text: The most recent iteration of the immersive theater experience Sleep No More, which premiered in New York City in 2011, transforms its performance space — a five-story warehouse — into a 1930s-era hotel. Audience members, who wander through the labyrinthine venue at their own pace and follow the actors as they play out simultaneous, interweaving narrative loops, confront the impossibility of experiencing the production in its entirety. Choice A is incorrect. The fact that the venue is in New York City isn’t connected to the experimental nature of the performance. It’s the size of the venue, not its location in New York, that affects the theatrical experience. Choice B is incorrect. The text never suggests that audience members are disappointed because they can’t see the entire production. In fact, it suggests that that’s an important part of the experience. stimulus.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

The nautical mile (6,076 feet) is the measure of distance used in seafaring navigation. A nautical mile directly correlates to one minute (1/60th of a degree) of latitude. The curvature of Earth affects the accurate measurement of long distances when using flat maps. Measuring distances with latitude and longitude coordinates takes into account Earth’s curvature. Mariners use nautical charts marked with latitude and longitude to quickly calculate distances and positions.

stem.text: The student wants to explain why nautical miles are used to measure distances in seafaring navigation. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nautical miles are a measure of distance equal to one minute of latitude, which is a feature nautical charts use to calculate distances and positions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Since they directly correlate to the coordinates on nautical charts, which take into account Earth’s curvature, nautical miles are an efficient way to calculate distances at sea.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Using nautical miles for navigation at sea takes Earth’s curvature into account, whereas measuring distances with latitude and longitude coordinates does not.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nautical charts use latitude and longitude to measure long distances; these charts are more accurate than flat maps for measuring distances in seafaring navigation because they account for Earth’s curvature.

explanation.text:
Choice B is the best answer. The sentence explains why nautical miles are used to measure distances in seafaring navigation, noting that they directly correlate to the coordinates on nautical charts that take into account Earth’s curvature, making them an efficient way to calculate distances at sea.

Choice A is incorrect. While the sentence describes what nautical miles are and their relationship to nautical charts, it doesn’t explain why nautical miles are used to measure distances in seafaring navigation. Choice C is incorrect. While the sentence indicates a reason why nautical miles are used, it misrepresents information from the notes: measuring distances with latitude and longitude does in fact account for Earth’s curvature. Choice D is incorrect. The sentence explains why nautical charts are more accurate than flat maps; it doesn’t explain why nautical miles specifically are used to measure distances in seafaring navigation.

stem.text: On March 27, 2004, after nine years as a professional boxer, Isra Girgrah retired. The Yemeni American athlete ______ her career with a record of twenty-eight wins, three losses, and two ties. Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

stimulus.text: Marta Coll and colleagues’ 2010 Mediterranean Sea biodiversity census reported approximately 17,000 species, nearly double the number reported in Carlo Bianchi and Carla Morri’s 2000 census — a difference only partly attributable to the description of new invertebrate species in the interim. stem.text: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Coll and colleagues reported a much higher number of species than Bianchi and Morri did largely due to the inclusion of invertebrate species that had not been described at the time of Bianchi and Morri’s census.

choices.label: B
choices.text: some differences observed in microorganisms may have been treated as variations within species by Bianchi and Morri but treated as indicative of distinct species by Coll and colleagues.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bianchi and Morri may have been less sensitive to the degree of morphological variation displayed within a typical species of microorganism than Coll and colleagues were.

choices.label: D
choices.text: the absence of clarity regarding how to differentiate among species of microorganisms may have resulted in Coll and colleagues underestimating the number of microorganism species.

explanation.text:
Choice B is the best answer because it presents the conclusion that most logically completes the text’s discussion of the different counts of species in the Mediterranean Sea. The text states that Coll and colleagues reported almost double the number of species that Bianchi and Morri reported in their study ten years earlier. According to the text, this difference can only be partly attributed to new invertebrate species being described in the years between the two studies, which means there must be an additional factor that made Coll and colleagues’ count so much higher than Bianchi and Morri’s count. The text goes on to explain that factor: researchers have a relatively poor understanding of microorganisms’ morphological variability, or the differences in microorganisms’ structure and form. This poor understanding makes it hard to classify microorganisms by species and means that researchers’ decisions about classifying microorganisms can have a large effect on the overall species counts that researchers report. Additionally, the text says that the two censuses reported similar numbers of vertebrate, plant, and algal species, which means that the difference in overall species did not come from differences in those categories. Given all this information, it most logically follows that Coll and colleagues may have treated some of the differences among microorganisms as indicative of the microorganisms being different species, whereas Bianchi and Morri treated those differences as variations within species, resulting in Coll and colleagues reporting many more species than Bianchi and Morri did.

Choice A is incorrect because the text explicitly addresses this issue by stating that the description of new invertebrate species in the years between the two studies can explain only part of the difference in the number of species reported by the studies. The focus of the text is on explaining the difference between Coll and colleagues’ count and Bianchi and Morri’s count that cannot be accounted for by the inclusion of invertebrate species that had not been described at the time of Bianchi and Morri’s study. Choice C is incorrect because nothing in the text suggests that Bianchi and Morri may have been less sensitive to how much the form and structure of microorganisms vary within the same species than Coll and colleagues were. If Bianchi and Morri had been less sensitive to within-species variation than Coll and colleagues were, Bianchi and Morri would likely have reported more species than Coll and colleagues did, since less sensitivity to within-species variation would lead researchers to classify as different species microorganisms that more sensitive researchers would classify as variations within the same species. The text indicates, however, that Bianchi and Morri reported far fewer species than Coll and colleagues did; since the text also excludes other explanations for this difference, it suggests that in fact Bianchi and Morri were more sensitive to within-species variation than Coll and colleagues were, leading Bianchi and Morri to report fewer overall species. Choice D is incorrect because the text is focused on explaining why Coll and colleagues reported many more species than Bianchi and Morri did, and an underestimate of the number of microorganism species by Coll and colleagues would not explain that difference — it would suggest, in fact, that the difference in the number of species should have been even larger.

Choice A is incorrect because it results in a rhetorically unacceptable sentence fragment beginning with "on" and separates a necessary preposition from the clause beginning with "there." Choice B is incorrect because a semicolon can’t be used in this way to join the main clause ("there...on") and the supplementary phrase ("openness to experience"). A semicolon is conventionally used to join two main clauses, whereas a colon is conventionally used to introduce an element that explains or amplifies the information in the preceding clause, making the colon the better choice in this context. Choice C is incorrect because it fails to mark the boundary between the main clause ("there...on") and the supplementary phrase ("openness to experience").

stimulus.text: In his Naturalis historia, Pliny the Elder praised Hipparchus’s star catalog, a second-century BCE list of roughly 850 different stars’ celestial positions. For centuries, scholars dreamed about locating a copy of this legendary lost ______ fantasy (partially) became reality in 2022, when researchers uncovered traces of the star catalog on a palimpsest, a reused parchment.

stem.text: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

explanation.text:
Choice C is the best answer. The convention being tested is punctuation use between sentences. In this choice, the period is used correctly to mark the boundary between one sentence ("For … work") and another ("That … parchment").

Choice A is incorrect because it results in a comma splice. A comma can’t be used in this way to mark the boundary between sentences. Choice B is incorrect because it results in a run-on sentence. The sentences ("For … work" and "that … parchment") are fused without punctuation and/or a conjunction. Choice D is incorrect. Without a comma preceding it, the conjunction "and" can’t be used in this way to join sentences.

stimulus.text: The city of Pompeii, which was buried in ash following the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE, continues to be studied by archaeologists. Unfortunately, as ______ attest, archaeological excavations have disrupted ash deposits at the site, causing valuable information about the eruption to be lost.

stem.text: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.label: A
choices.text: researchers, Roberto Scandone and Christopher Kilburn,

choices.label: B
choices.text: researchers, Roberto Scandone and Christopher Kilburn

choices.label: C
choices.text: researchers Roberto Scandone and Christopher Kilburn

choices.label: D
choices.text: researchers Roberto Scandone, and Christopher Kilburn

explanation.text:
Choice C is the best answer. The convention being tested is the punctuation of a restrictive coordinated noun phrase. No punctuation is needed within or around the coordinated noun phrase “researchers Roberto Scandone and Christopher Kilburn” because it would create an illogical separation between the noun “researchers” and the coordinated noun phrase “Roberto Scandone and Christopher Kilburn.”

Choice A is incorrect because no punctuation is needed. Placing a pair of commas around the coordinated noun phrase “Roberto Scandone and Christopher Kilburn” creates an illogical separation between the noun “researchers” and the aforementioned coordinated noun phrase. In this case, it illogically suggests that researchers in general bear the specific names Roberto Scandone and Christopher Kilburn. Choice B is incorrect because no punctuation is needed between the noun “researchers” and the coordinated noun phrase “Roberto Scandone and Christopher Kilburn.” Choice D is incorrect because no punctuation is needed within the coordinated noun phrase “Roberto Scandone and Christopher Kilburn.”

stem.text: The Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI), a commonly used measure of competition between companies in a particular market, ranges from a score of zero to 10,000 points. Compared with that of a highly concentrated market — that is, a market controlled by very few companies — ______ Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.label: A
choices.text: a market that is less concentrated will have a much lower HHI score.

choices.label: B
choices.text: the HHI score of a less concentrated market will be much lower.

choices.label: C
choices.text: when a market is less concentrated, its HHI score will be much lower.

choices.label: D
choices.text: a less concentrated market will have an HHI score that is much lower.

explanation.text:
Choice B is the best answer. The convention being tested is subject-modifier placement. This choice makes the noun phrase "the HHI...market" the subject of the sentence and places it immediately after the modifying phrase "compared...market." In doing so, this choice clearly establishes that the HHI score of a less concentrated market — and not another noun in the sentence — is being compared with the HHI score of a highly concentrated market.

Choice A is incorrect because it results in a dangling modifier. The placement of "a market that is less concentrated" immediately after the modifying phrase illogically suggests that a market is being compared with an HHI score. Choice C is incorrect because it results in a confusing, illogical sentence. The placement of the modifier "when a market is less concentrated" after "a highly concentrated market" is contradictory. Furthermore, it’s ambiguous what "its" is referring to in "its HHI score," resulting in an illogical comparison. Choice D is incorrect because it results in a dangling modifier. The placement of "a less concentrated market" immediately after the modifying phrase illogically suggests that a market is being compared with an HHI score.

stem.text: Quantum particles of light — photons — provide an unhackable means of transmitting encryption keys over networks, as attempts to observe particles in quantum states will invariably alter the particles ______ dismantle any information they transmit. Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

explanation.text:
Choice B is the best answer. This choice uses paired punctuation in the form of two commas to set off the nonessential phrase "in the process."

Choice A is incorrect. The phrase "in the process" is a nonessential element and needs to be set off with paired punctuation. We need a comma after "and" to match the one after "process." Choice C is incorrect. The phrase "in the process" is a nonessential element and needs to be set off with paired punctuation, so we would need a dash after "and" to match the one following "process." Choice D is incorrect. The phrase "in the process" is a nonessential element and needs to be set off with paired punctuation. We would need a comma after "process" to match the one following "and."

stem.text: In ancient Greece, an Epicurean was a follower of Epicurus, a philosopher whose beliefs revolved around the pursuit of pleasure. Epicurus defined pleasure as “the absence of pain in the body and of trouble in the ______ that all life’s virtues derived from this absence. Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

explanation.text:
Choice A is the best answer. The convention being tested is punctuation use between a main clause and a participial phrase. This choice correctly uses a comma to mark the boundary between the main clause (“Epicurus …‘soul’”) and the participial phrase (“positing … absence”) that provides additional information about how Epicurus defined pleasure.

Choice B is incorrect because a colon can’t be used in this way to join a main clause and a participial phrase. Choice C is incorrect because a semicolon can’t be used in this way to join a main clause and a participial phrase. Choice D is incorrect because it results in a rhetorically unacceptable sentence fragment beginning with “positing.”

stimulus.text: The Kaiparowits Formation is a fossil-rich layer of sedimentary rock in the Grand Staircase, a colossal sequence of rock layers stretching from Utah’s Bryce Canyon to Arizona’s Grand Canyon. The sandstones and mudstones of the Kaiparowits Formation were deposited ______ the Late Cretaceous, preserving many species from that time.

stem.text: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

explanation.text:
Choice D is the best answer. The convention being tested is punctuation use between a preposition and its complement. No punctuation is needed between the preposition “during” and its complement “the Late Cretaceous.” The complement completes the meaning of the preposition in the phrase “deposited during the Late Cretaceous,” and any punctuation between the two results in an ungrammatical sentence.

Choice A is incorrect because no punctuation is needed between the preposition and its complement. Choice B is incorrect because no punctuation is needed between the preposition and its complement. Choice C is incorrect because no punctuation is needed between the preposition and its complement.

stem.text: American poet Emily Dickinson wrote many of her poems on scraps of paper, but she also took steps to collect these works. From 1858 to around 1864, for example, she copied more than 800 of ______ into forty homemade booklets (known as fascicles). Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

explanation.text:
Choice A is the best answer. The pronoun "them" agrees with the plural antecedents "poems" and "works."

Choice B is incorrect. "This" is a singular pronoun, but its antecedents, "poems" and "works," are plural. Choice C is incorrect. "That" is a singular pronoun, but its antecedents, "poems" and "works," are plural. Choice D is incorrect. "It" is a singular pronoun, but its antecedents, "poems" and "works," are plural.

stem.text: Researchers studying turnout found that a large share of registered voters chose to ______ from the referendum entirely, neither supporting nor opposing the measure.

explanation.text: *ab-* (away) + *ten* (hold): hold yourself away from the vote. *Abdicate* is giving up an office. Also in play: *accede* (*ad-* + *ced*), *contravene* (*contra-* + *ven*).

stem.text: Because certain proteins have a strong ______ for zinc ions, they bind the metal even when it is present only in trace amounts.

explanation.text: *ad-/af-* (toward): a pull toward something. *Aversion* and *antipathy* are the exact opposite direction — that is the elimination the prefix buys you.

stem.text: Rather than challenge the trade restriction directly, the company found a legal way to ______ it, routing shipments through a third country.

explanation.text: *circum-* (around) + *ven* (come): going around the rule. *Subvert* (*sub-* + *vert*) means undermining it from below, which the company is not doing.

stem.text: The interviewer's deliberately neutral phrasing was designed to ______ detailed accounts from witnesses without suggesting what they ought to say.

explanation.text: *e-* (out) + *lic*: draw out, specifically by questioning. *Evoke* calls forth a feeling or memory, not information; *extract* implies force the neutral phrasing rules out.

stem.text: The sulfurous smell of the hot springs ______ the entire valley, lingering even on windy days.

explanation.text: *per-* (through). *Dispersed* moves outward and thins; the smell here saturates and stays.

stem.text: A clause in the original bequest ______ any future resale of the collection, so the museum could not have sold the paintings even had it wanted to.

explanation.text: *pre-* (before) + *clud* (shut): shut off in advance. *Protracted* and *prolonged* are about length, not prevention.

stem.text: Once the invasive algae reached the warmer northern waters, it began to ______, doubling its coverage in a single season.

explanation.text: *pro-* (forward) + *fer* (carry). Three distractors all mean decrease — a clean positive/negative split.

stem.text: Under pressure from the tribunal, the astronomer publicly ______ his earlier claim, though his private letters suggest he never abandoned it.

explanation.text: *re-* (back) + *cant* (sing): take the claim back. *Reiterated* is the trap if you only register the *re-*; it means repeated, the opposite of what the tribunal wanted.

stem.text: Digital cameras did not merely compete with film; within a decade they had almost entirely ______ it in consumer markets.

explanation.text: *sub-* (from below) + *plant*: displaced and took the place of. *Surmounted* (*super-*) means overcame an obstacle, which film is not.

stem.text: The editor cut three paragraphs she considered ______: they restated information the reader had already been given twice.

explanation.text: *super-* (over) + *flu* (flow): overflowing, more than needed. *Tangential* is the strong trap — repeated material is redundant, not off-topic.

stem.text: The colony's presence on the island was ______; the birds arrived in April and were gone before the end of June.

explanation.text: *trans-* (across) + *i* (go): passing through. *Intermittent* describes a stop-start pattern; this is one short stay.

stem.text: A redesigned drainage system would ______ the need for the emergency pumps altogether, making them unnecessary rather than merely less frequently used.

explanation.text: *ob-* (in the way) + *via* (road). Note that *alleviate*, *mitigate*, and *palliate* all mean reduce — the sentence explicitly demands eliminate ("rather than merely less frequently used"). A two-constraint question hiding in Set A.

stem.text: The committee asked the author to strip out ______ material — anecdotes and asides that, however charming, had nothing to do with the argument.

explanation.text: *extra-* (outside). *Germane* means relevant, the opposite; *intrinsic* and *inherent* (*intra-*, within) point inward.

stem.text: The penalty could not be applied ______: conduct that had been legal when it occurred remained legal in the eyes of the court.

explanation.text: *retro-* (backward). *Posthumously* (*post-*, after death) is a decoy for anyone matching only "after."

stem.text: The trial results were ______: the drug outperformed the placebo on one measure and underperformed it on another, so no clear conclusion could be drawn.

explanation.text: *equi-* (equal) + *voc* (voice): two voices of equal weight. *Unequivocal* is the same root with a negating prefix and means the opposite.

stem.text: Although the board's public statement implied ______ support, the minutes record that two members voted against the proposal.

explanation.text: *uni-* (one) + *anim* (spirit). *Tacit* means unspoken, which the minutes contradict.

stem.text: Where the river once ran as a single channel, sediment deposits have caused it to ______, splitting the flow into two branches.

explanation.text: *bi-* (two). *Coalesce* (*co-*, together) and *converge* both merge rather than split.

stem.text: Raccoons thrive in cities partly because they are ______, willing to eat everything from crayfish to discarded pizza.

explanation.text: *omni-* (all) + *vor* (eat). The other two *omni-* words are there precisely to test whether you read past the prefix.

stem.text: The manuscript is missing only its ______ page; the final page, bearing the author's signature, survives intact.

explanation.text: *pen-* (almost) + *ultim* (last): second to last. *Ultimate* is contradicted by the surviving final page.

stem.text: The senator's remarks about her opponent were surprisingly ______ given how bitter the campaign had become — mild, even complimentary.

explanation.text: *bene-* (good). *Malevolent* and *malignant* are the *mal-* mirror; *belligerent* (*bell*, war) fits the campaign but not "mild, even complimentary."

stem.text: The auditor's report distinguished honest bookkeeping errors from outright ______: deliberate misuse of public funds by officials who knew better.

explanation.text: *mal-* (bad) + *fac* (do): deliberate wrongdoing in office. *Negligence* and *inadvertence* are the honest errors the sentence contrasts against.

stem.text: Once the transfer is confirmed the decision is ______; there is no mechanism by which the donor can call the gift back.

explanation.text: *ir-* (not) + *re-* (back) + *voc* (call): cannot be called back. *Immutable* means cannot be changed in form — close, but the sentence is specifically about reclaiming.

stem.text: Though the archive's contents are water-damaged and disorganized, historians consider them ______: no other record of the settlement survives.

explanation.text: The *in-* trap from the reference: here it intensifies rather than negates. *Valueless* is what the prefix looks like it should mean.

stem.text: The dataset combined ______ sources — census records, ship manifests, and parish registers — that had never before been analyzed together.

explanation.text: *dis-* (apart). *Analogous* and *homogeneous* claim similarity, which the list of unlike sources rules out.

stem.text: The finding is ______: adding a fourth lane to the highway lengthened average commute times rather than shortening them.

explanation.text: *counter-* (against). *Self-evident* is its opposite.

stem.text: Two independent teams using different instruments ______ the original measurement, making the result far harder to dismiss.

explanation.text: *co-* (together) + *robor* (strength): two teams strengthening one result. *Refuted* is the trap for anyone reading "different instruments" as conflict.

stem.text: Interviewers found the physicist frustratingly ______: he answered most questions in three or four words and volunteered nothing further.

explanation.text: Sparing with words. Every other choice — *loquacious*, *verbose*, *garrulous* (*loqu*, *verb*) — means the opposite, so the roots do all the elimination for you.

stem.text: The proposal met ______ opposition at the town meeting, with residents shouting objections over one another for nearly an hour.

explanation.text: *voc* (voice) + *fer* (carry). *Tacit*, *muted*, and *tepid* all fail on "shouting."

stem.text: The two accounts ______ each other on a key detail: one places the ship in port on the 14th, the other at sea.

explanation.text: *contra-* (against) + *dict* (say). *Contravene* is the near-miss: you contravene a rule or treaty, not another account.

stem.text: The charter ______ the governor's authority, limiting it to matters explicitly listed in Article II.

explanation.text: *circum-* (around) + *scrib* (write): a boundary drawn around it. *Prescribed* would mean dictated the authority, not limited it.

stem.text: "Koala bear" is a ______: the animal is a marsupial and no relation to bears at all.

explanation.text: *nom* (name): the wrong name. *Euphemism* and *hyperbole* describe how something is said, not that it is misnamed.

stem.text: The editors gave little ______ to the anonymous tip until a second source produced documents supporting it.

explanation.text: *cred* (believe). *Deference* (*de-* + *fer*, yielding to authority) is the strongest distractor and means something quite different.

stem.text: Written in 1954, the essay now looks ______: it anticipated both networked computing and the privacy problems that would follow.

explanation.text: *pre-* (before) + *sci* (know). *Omniscient* is the same root overshot: the essay predicted two things, not everything.

stem.text: The company insists that its executives were not ______ of the safety reports, though internal emails suggest otherwise.

explanation.text: *cogn* (know). *Culpable* (*culp*, blame) is what the emails imply, but the sentence is about knowledge, not fault.

stem.text: Critics ______ the failure to the director personally, though she had opposed the plan from the outset.

explanation.text: *in-* + *put* (reckon): assign responsibility to. *Exonerate* runs the opposite direction.

stem.text: Although a ______ has formed around the broad outline of the theory, specialists continue to argue about the mechanism.

explanation.text: *con-* (together) + *sent* (feel). *Dissent* is the same root with the opposite prefix, and the "although" makes it tempting.

stem.text: Historians praise the city's ______ planning: reservoirs built in the 1920s, when water seemed abundant, are what carried the region through the recent drought.

explanation.text: *pro-* (ahead) + *vid* (see): seeing ahead. *Improvident* is the negation; *inadvertent* would make the foresight accidental, which the praise contradicts.

stem.text: Her ______ reading of the ledgers caught a discrepancy that three previous auditors had missed.

explanation.text: *per-* (thoroughly) + *spic* (look). *Cursory* (*curs*, run) is exactly the wrong intensity — a quick reading misses discrepancies rather than catching them.

stem.text: Given how little was known about the drug's long-term effects, the physicians were ______ in their recommendations, avoiding any firm endorsement.

explanation.text: *circum-* + *spect* (look around before acting). *Presumptuous* and *zealous* both overstep, which "avoiding any firm endorsement" excludes.

stem.text: The second edition adds a dozen diagrams meant to ______ the argument for readers without a statistics background.

explanation.text: *luc* (light): to shed light on. *Obfuscate* darkens; *attenuate* weakens.

stem.text: The orphaned foals proved unexpectedly ______, allowing handlers to fit halters within days of their arrival.

explanation.text: *doc* (teach) + *-ile* (tending toward): teachable. *Recalcitrant* and *obstinate* mean stubbornly resistant, and *torpid* means sluggish — none of which lets handlers work in days.

stem.text: The plaque does not celebrate the battle so much as ______ the civilians who died in it.

explanation.text: *com-* + *mem* (remember). *Extol* and *venerate* mean praise, but the sentence explicitly refuses celebration.

stem.text: The floodwaters took nearly a week to ______, leaving a layer of silt across the fields.

explanation.text: *re-* (back) + *ced* (go). *Concede*, *accede*, and *secede* share the root and go every other direction.

stem.text: Because no court had ruled on a case of this kind before, the decision established a ______ that later judges would be obliged to weigh.

explanation.text: *pre-* + *ced*: the case that goes before. *Premise* is a starting assumption in an argument, not a model for later decisions.

stem.text: The lecturer had a habit of ______, wandering into stories about his graduate school days before returning, eventually, to the topic.

explanation.text: *dis-* (apart) + *gress* (step): stepping away and returning. *Transgressing* means violating a rule.

stem.text: The union asked a federal mediator to ______ once talks between the two sides broke down completely.

explanation.text: *inter-* (between) + *ven* (come). All four choices share *ven*; only the prefix separates them, which is the whole point of the question.

stem.text: Rainfall in the region is ______ rather than seasonal: storms arrive at unpredictable intervals with long dry spells between them.

explanation.text: *inter-* + *mit* (send): sending, stopping, sending again. *Incessant* and *perpetual* mean never stopping.

stem.text: Junior researchers often ______ to senior colleagues on questions of method, even when the data suggest a different approach.

explanation.text: *de-* (down) + *fer* (carry): yield to. The other three *fer* words are all about information moving, not authority yielding.

stem.text: The letter ______ to be a firsthand account of the expedition, but its author never left London.

explanation.text: *pro-* (forward) + *port* (carry): puts itself forward as. *Comports* means behaves or accords with.

stem.text: From a handful of fossilized footprints, the team was able to ______ the animal's approximate weight and gait.

explanation.text: *de-* (down from) + *duc* (lead): lead down from evidence to conclusion. *Adduce* means to cite evidence, not to derive from it.

stem.text: The dispute has proved ______: four rounds of negotiation across eleven years have produced no agreement at all.

explanation.text: *in-* (not) + *tract* (pull): cannot be pulled into shape. *Protracted* fits "eleven years" perfectly and ignores "no agreement at all" — a half-fit answer, exactly the pattern to watch.

stem.text: The evidence does not ______ the conclusion the authors draw; it merely makes that conclusion one possibility among several.

explanation.text: *com-* + *pel* (drive): drive you to the conclusion. The other three *pel* words all push away.

stem.text: Without written records from the period, historians can only ______ about how the settlement was governed.

explanation.text: *con-* + *ject* (throw): throw a guess together. *Corroborate*, *substantiate*, and *verify* all require the evidence the sentence says does not exist.

stem.text: Emergency releases from the upstream dam ______ the flooding that forecasters had predicted for the delta.

explanation.text: *ab-* (away) + *vert* (turn): turned it aside. *Subverted* undermines something, and floods are not undermined.

stem.text: Reviewers criticized the paper's ______ structure: the central claim does not appear until page 14, after three unrelated digressions.

explanation.text: *con-* + *volut* (roll): rolled up on itself. *Lucid* and *succinct* are what the reviewers say it is not.

stem.text: An unexpected ______ of migrating birds overwhelmed the sanctuary's monitoring stations that autumn.

explanation.text: *in-* (into) + *flu* (flow). *Dearth* is scarcity — the opposite — and *exodus* flows outward.

stem.text: The disease is easiest to treat in its ______ stage, before symptoms become pronounced enough to prompt a visit to a doctor.

explanation.text: *in-* + *cip* (take): just taking hold. *Chronic* and *terminal* are late stages; *recurrent* describes a pattern, not a stage.

stem.text: Once a third experiment failed to reproduce the effect, the original hypothesis became ______.

explanation.text: *un-* + *ten* (hold): cannot be held. *Tenuous* is the sharp near-miss — a tenuous hypothesis is weak but still standing, whereas a failed replication puts this one past defending.

stem.text: The committee described the lapse as ______ — not merely careless, but deserving of formal censure.

explanation.text: *re-* + *prehend* (grasp): grasping it back for condemnation. The dash construction requires more than carelessness, which kills *inadvertent* and *negligible*.

stem.text: Because the reagent degrades quickly, the protocol imposes ______ limits on how long samples may sit before analysis.

explanation.text: *string* (bind tight). *Lenient* is the opposite and *arbitrary* contradicts the stated reason.

stem.text: The monastery was deliberately ______, built on a ridge two days' walk from the nearest village.

explanation.text: *se-* (apart) + *clud* (shut). *Precluded* is the same root doing a different job — it needs an object like "any resale."

stem.text: Juveniles of the species show a marked ______ for investigating novel objects, a tendency that fades in adulthood.

explanation.text: *pro-* + *pend* (hang toward): a leaning. Everything else is an absence of leaning or an obstacle.

stem.text: The composer's style is ______, drawing on Appalachian fiddle tunes, Javanese gamelan, and mid-century serialism within a single piece.

explanation.text: *ex-* (out) + *lect* (choose): chosen from many sources. *Derivative* implies copying one source; *doctrinaire* (*doct*) means rigidly committed to one school.

stem.text: Over four decades she was extraordinarily ______, publishing more than sixty novels alongside her academic work.

explanation.text: *pro-* (forward) + *fic* (make). *Meticulous* describes care, not output; *eminent* describes reputation.

stem.text: The vaccine proved ______ against the variant, reducing severe cases by more than 80 percent in the trial.

explanation.text: *ex-* + *fic* (make): producing the intended effect. *Efficient* means without waste of resources, which a trial result does not measure — a precise distinction the SAT likes.

stem.text: The situation was ______ enough that the council waived its usual thirty-day review period.

explanation.text: *ex-* + *ag* (drive): pressing, demanding action now. *Contingent* means dependent on something else.

stem.text: Without enforcement authority the commission was effectively ______: it could publish findings but compel nothing.

explanation.text: *im-* (not) + *pot* (power). *Omnipotent* is the same root inverted, and *impartial* is a plausible-sounding word that has nothing to do with enforcement.

stem.text: Readers of her letters find her ______ about fame: she courted attention in public and complained bitterly about it in private.

explanation.text: *ambi-* (both) + *val* (strength): two opposing pulls of equal force. *Indifferent* and *apathetic* mean no feeling at all, which "complained bitterly" rules out. *Equivocal*, had it appeared, would describe vague language rather than divided feeling.

stem.text: The dinners were famously ______: long, loud, and full of argument that never quite curdled into quarrel.

explanation.text: *con-* (together) + *viv* (life). *Somber* and *staid* are the opposite mood.

stem.text: By 1890 the industry was ______: three of the four mills had closed and the last was operating two days a week.

explanation.text: *mor* (death) + *-bund*: dying. *Nascent* and *burgeoning* describe beginnings, which the closures contradict.

stem.text: The field was still ______ in 1975 — a handful of researchers, no journals, and no agreed vocabulary.

explanation.text: *nasc* (born): just born. *Entrenched* and *preeminent* both imply an establishment the sentence says did not exist.

stem.text: The reforms ______ a wave of imitation across neighboring states, most of which passed similar measures within three years.

explanation.text: *en-* + *gen* (birth): gave rise to. *Precluded* and *obviated* would prevent the imitation the sentence says occurred.

stem.text: In victory he was ______, praising at length the opponent he had spent six months attacking.

explanation.text: *magn* (great) + *anim* (spirit). *Ingratiating* (*grat*) implies angling for favor; a victor praising a defeated opponent gains nothing.

stem.text: The rain gave the firefighters only a brief ______; by evening the winds had returned and the fire resumed its advance.

explanation.text: *re-* + *spir* (breathe): a breathing space. *Impasse* is a deadlock, and *resurgence* describes what the fire does afterward, not what the rain gives.

stem.text: Medieval theologians argued at length about whether angels possessed ______ form or existed as pure intellect.

explanation.text: *corp* (body). *Ephemeral* concerns duration, not physicality.

stem.text: Her ______ use of the limited budget — repairs first, cosmetic improvements never — kept the theater open through the recession.

explanation.text: *jud* (judge). *Capricious* and *arbitrary* mean the reverse; *profligate* (wastefully extravagant) contradicts "limited budget."

stem.text: The letters reveal an official of unusual ______: he refused gifts from contractors at a time when nearly everyone accepted them.

explanation.text: *prob* (test, prove) + *-ity*: proven integrity. *Acumen* is shrewdness and *affability* is friendliness — neither is what refusing gifts demonstrates.

stem.text: New forensic analysis ______ the man convicted in 1987, showing that the fibers used against him could not have come from his coat.

explanation.text: *ex-* (out of) + *culp* (blame). *Implicated* and *indicted* (*in-* + *dict*) run the opposite direction.

stem.text: Because enforcement was so lax, factories dumped waste into the river with near ______ for decades.

explanation.text: *im-* (not) + *pun* (punishment): without punishment. *Immunity* is the trap — immunity is a formal legal exemption, while impunity is simply escaping consequences in practice, which is what lax enforcement produces.

stem.text: The audit identified the error in 2019, but no one moved to ______ it until customers began complaining publicly.

explanation.text: *rect* (straight) + *-fy* (make): make it right. *Ratify* means formally approve; *relegate* means demote.

stem.text: The treaty was not renegotiated but simply ______: the new government declared it void and stopped observing its terms.

explanation.text: *ab-* (away) + *rog* (ask): repealed unilaterally. *Ratified* and *invoked* both affirm the treaty; *amended* implies the renegotiation the sentence rules out.

stem.text: Rather than approve each purchase himself, the director ______ that authority to department heads.

explanation.text: *de-* + *leg* (law, assign): handed authority downward. *Relegated* demotes, *abdicated* gives up the office entirely, and *arrogated* (*ad-* + *rog*) claims authority for oneself — four different fates for a power, and only one matches.

stem.text: The report loses itself in ______ — three pages on font choice, one paragraph on the budget shortfall.

explanation.text: *min* (small). *Conjecture* and *hyperbole* describe kinds of claim, not triviality.

stem.text: Rather than ______ the shortage, the emergency subsidy worsened it by encouraging households to stockpile.

explanation.text: *ad-* + *lev* (light): lighten. Careful with the construction — "rather than ______, it worsened it" means the blank is the *good* outcome, so *aggravate* (*grav*, heavy) and *exacerbate* are both backwards.

stem.text: The eulogy balanced grief with moments of ______, drawing laughter from mourners who had been weeping minutes earlier.

explanation.text: *lev* (light) — lightness of mood. *Gravity* and *solemnity* are the weight the eulogy is being balanced against.

stem.text: The archive is ______ with material on the war years but contains almost nothing from the decade preceding them.

explanation.text: *re-* + *plet* (full). *Depleted* is the same root emptied out.

stem.text: The speech was polished and ______: forty minutes of rising cadence around no identifiable proposal.

explanation.text: *vac* (empty) + *-ous* (full of): full of emptiness. *Incisive* and *trenchant* mean sharp and substantive; *succinct* is contradicted by forty minutes.

stem.text: The pigment is ______ — brilliant when first applied, but faded to gray within a few years of exposure to light.

explanation.text: *van* (empty) + *-escent* (becoming): fading away. *Indelible* and *immutable* both mean it would not change.

stem.text: After the mine closed the town was left ______: shuttered storefronts, an empty school, and fewer than a hundred residents.

explanation.text: *sol* (alone). *Tranquil* and *placid* are calm in a pleasant sense — an emptied-out mining town is not peaceful, it is abandoned.

stem.text: The technique was genuinely ______ in 1962, though it is standard equipment in every lab today.

explanation.text: *nov* (new). *Rudimentary* means basic, and *quotidian* means everyday — both plausible-sounding, neither meaning new.

stem.text: The company's ______ in the market lasted precisely as long as its patents did.

explanation.text: *prim* (first). *Parity* means equality with rivals, which is the opposite of what patents confer.

stem.text: The two firms parted ways ______, dividing the assets in a single afternoon and issuing a joint statement.

explanation.text: *am* (love). *Acrimoniously* is the antonym the single-afternoon division rules out.

stem.text: The translation is praised for its ______ to the original's rhythm, even where that required departing from the literal sense.

explanation.text: *fid* (faith): faithfulness to the original. *Deference* would mean yielding to it, and *proximity* is mere closeness.

stem.text: Though widely regarded as the finest mathematician of her generation, she was ______ in seminars, rarely speaking unless asked a direct question.

explanation.text: *dis-* + *fid* (faith): lacking confidence in oneself. *Indifferent* is the classic misread — she is not uninterested, she is shy.

stem.text: Reviewers objected to the novel's ______ violence: scenes that advanced neither plot nor character and seemed included for shock alone.

explanation.text: *grat*: given freely, and so unearned or unnecessary. *Gratifying* is the same root with the opposite slant.

stem.text: The error was ______ — not a rounding difference but a figure off by three orders of magnitude.

explanation.text: *e-* (out of) + *greg* (flock): standing out from the herd, and always for bad reasons. *Negligible* and *marginal* are what a rounding difference would be.

stem.text: Early geologists assumed the continents were ______; plate tectonics replaced that assumption with one of constant, imperceptible motion.

explanation.text: *im-* (not) + *mut* (change). *Impervious* means unaffected by outside force, which is not the assumption tectonics overturned.

stem.text: Asked to fill ten unexpected minutes, she gave an ______ talk that much of the audience assumed had been prepared for weeks.

explanation.text: *ex-* + *tempor* (time): out of the moment, unrehearsed. *Contemporaneous* is the same root meaning "at the same time" and is a pure form trap.

stem.text: The mayor promised to ______ permitting for rebuilt homes, cutting the average wait from nine months to six weeks.

explanation.text: *ex-* + *ped* (foot): free the feet, speed it up. *Impede* is the same root obstructed.

stem.text: The blight first ______ itself as a change in leaf color, weeks before any effect on yield could be measured.

explanation.text: *man* (hand) + *fest*: made visible. *Belied* would mean it disguised the blight rather than revealed it.

stem.text: Beneath the treaty's language of friendship lay obvious ______: neither side had surrendered its claim to the border province.

explanation.text: *dis-* (apart) + *cord* (heart). "Beneath the language of friendship" signals the contrast, so *concord* fits only the surface half of the sentence.

stem.text: His memos were ______ to the point of embarrassment, opening with two paragraphs praising whichever executive he happened to be writing to.

explanation.text: *ob-* + *sequ* (follow): following fawningly. *Circumspect* is cautious, not flattering.

stem.text: The road to the observatory is ______, climbing four thousand feet through more than fifty switchbacks.

explanation.text: *tort* (twist): full of twists. *Torturous* means causing torture — a one-letter difference the test genuinely uses. *Precipitous* covers only the steepness, not the switchbacks.

stem.text: Questions about the safety data were consistently ______: the spokesperson answered a slightly different question each time.

explanation.text: *de-* + *flect* (bend): bent aside. *Rebutted* and *refuted* would mean the spokesperson answered and disproved, which "a different question each time" denies.

stem.text: After three years the program had produced no ______ results — no measurable change in test scores, attendance, or graduation rates.

explanation.text: *tang* (touch): touchable, measurable. *Tacit* means unspoken and shares no meaning with it despite the near-identical opening.

stem.text: Her ______ note-taking across eleven field seasons produced the dataset that later researchers still rely on.

explanation.text: *ad-* + *sed* (sit): sitting steadily at the work. *Cursory*, *sporadic*, and *intermittent* would not produce a dataset anyone still relies on.

stem.text: The link between the two events is ______: a single undated letter that happens to mention both.

explanation.text: *ten* (stretch): stretched thin. One undated letter is the definition of thin evidence.

stem.text: The exhibition ______ the two artists' self-portraits, hanging them on facing walls so that visitors are forced to compare them.

explanation.text: *juxta* (beside) + *pos* (place). *Conflates* would merge the two, which facing walls specifically prevent.

stem.text: Editors were less concerned with the memoir's literary quality than with its ______: whether the events it describes actually occurred.

explanation.text: *ver* (true): actual truthfulness. *Verisimilitude* is the same root meaning only the *appearance* of truth — the correct word for fiction and the wrong one for a memoir's factual claims.

stem.text: Participants were told they could withdraw at any time, so their continued involvement was a matter of ______ rather than obligation.

explanation.text: *vol* (will). *Coercion* is the opposite and is what "could withdraw at any time" excludes.

stem.text: The delegation's tone was ______ from the opening minute: accusations, raised voices, and a threat to walk out.

explanation.text: *bell* (war). *Conciliatory* would be the peace-making counterpart.

stem.text: The colony is entirely ______, connected to the surface by a single ventilation shaft the ants keep clear.

explanation.text: *sub-* (under) + *terr* (earth). *Terrestrial* is the same root without the burial.

stem.text: Patients who are ______ within twenty-four hours of surgery recover measurably faster than those confined to bed.

explanation.text: *ambul* (walk). *Convalescent* (*con-* + *val*) describes recovering generally, but the sentence contrasts specifically with being confined to bed.

stem.text: The report described the oversight as a ______ error, one that cost the mission its primary instrument.

explanation.text: *grav/griev* (heavy, serious). *Inadvertent* addresses how the error happened, not how serious it was.

stem.text: The patient was still ______, strong enough to sit up but not to walk the length of the ward.

explanation.text: *-escent* (becoming) + *val* (strength): regaining strength. *Infirm* and *moribund* skip the recovery the sentence describes.

stem.text: The scheme proved ______: returns were paid out of new investors' deposits rather than from any profit.

explanation.text: *-ulent* (full of). *Redolent*, *benevolent*, and *prevalent* share the ending and share nothing else — pure suffix bait.

stem.text: What the memoir records is less talent than ______: eleven rejections, and a twelfth submission that finally sold.

explanation.text: *fort* (strong) + *-itude* (state of being). *Aptitude* is the "talent" the sentence explicitly sets aside.

stem.text: The inspection was ______ — ten minutes for a building that regulations say requires a full day.

explanation.text: *per-* + *funct* + *-ory*: going through the motions. *Rigorous* and *exhaustive* contradict ten minutes.

stem.text: The tone of the exchange was ______ rather than serious: name-calling, exaggerated sighs, and eye-rolling on both sides.

explanation.text: *-ile* (tending toward) + *puer* (child): childish. *Futile* and *volatile* share the ending only.

stem.text: Given how personal the attacks had become, her ______ was remarkable: she answered the substantive criticisms and ignored everything else.

explanation.text: *-ance* (state) + *fore-bear*: restraint under provocation. *Indifference* would mean she did not care, but she answered the substantive criticisms, so she did.

stem.text: She accepted the assignment with ______, volunteering before the request had been fully explained.

explanation.text: *-ity* (state of): cheerful readiness. *Equanimity* is calm, which does not explain volunteering early.

stem.text: Though the constitution named the emperor as head of state, power in the 1930s lay ______ with the military high command.

explanation.text: In practice though not in law. The sentence sets up the contrast with "though the constitution named" — *de jure* describes the emperor, not the generals.

stem.text: The argument is ______: it derives the result from the definitions alone, without appeal to any observation.

explanation.text: Reasoned from definitions rather than observation. *A posteriori* is its mirror and is exactly what "without appeal to any observation" excludes.

stem.text: Each time the model failed to predict an outcome, its defenders added an ______ assumption designed to explain away that single case.

explanation.text: Improvised for one specific case. *Ipso facto* is the sound-alike that means something entirely different.

stem.text: The reviewer's central complaint is that the conclusion is a ______: nothing in the preceding three chapters supports it.

explanation.text: A conclusion that does not follow. *Paradox* is self-contradiction and *tautology* is empty repetition — both real terms doing other jobs.

stem.text: Fossils are most informative when documented ______, since their orientation and surroundings carry as much information as the bones themselves.

explanation.text: In its original position. *Ex post facto* concerns retroactivity, not location.

stem.text: Access to clean water is treated in the report not as one goal among many but as a ______ for every other outcome it measures.

explanation.text: An indispensable condition. *Quid pro quo* is an exchange, and *status quo* is the current state.

stem.text: Locke's claim that the infant mind is a ______ has not survived contact with modern developmental psychology.

explanation.text: A blank slate. *Prima facie* concerns first appearances of evidence.

stem.text: The evidence is compelling ______, but the defense has not yet presented its case.

explanation.text: Compelling on its face, before the other side is heard — the second clause is what makes this the answer rather than *per se*.

stem.text: The witness's account was transcribed ______, including the false starts and repetitions.

explanation.text: Word for word, which false starts and repetitions confirm.

stem.text: Money in politics is not the problem ______; the problem is the absence of any rule governing who may give it.

explanation.text: In itself, intrinsically. *Ergo* is a connective meaning therefore and cannot occupy this slot.

stem.text: The authors attach one important ______ to their finding: the sample included only patients under forty.

explanation.text: A qualifying warning. *Corollary* is something that follows from the finding, and *premise* is what it started from.

stem.text: Three weeks of high fever left him ______, unable to climb a single flight of stairs without stopping to rest.

explanation.text: Drained of energy, despite looking like "energized." Every other choice means invigorated, so getting this wrong costs you the whole question.

stem.text: Her questions were ______ rather than pointed: she genuinely did not know what the acronym stood for.

explanation.text: Innocent, naive. *Ingenious* (clever) is the near-homograph and *disingenuous* is the negation — three of the four choices are the same trap in different clothes.

stem.text: Both parties agreed to submit the dispute to a ______ third party with no financial stake in the outcome.

explanation.text: Impartial, with no stake. *Uninterested* means bored, and the phrase "no financial stake" tells you which is wanted.

stem.text: The introduction's ______ praise — six paragraphs comparing the author to Darwin — made several reviewers uneasy.

explanation.text: Excessive to the point of insincerity — the reason reviewers were uneasy. If it merely meant abundant praise, there would be nothing to be uneasy about.

stem.text: The question left the candidate visibly ______: he opened his mouth twice and said nothing.

explanation.text: Bewildered, at a loss. *Unfazed* is what people wrongly assume it means, and the silence rules it out.

stem.text: The prose is competent but ______ — accurate sentences that never once surprise the reader.

explanation.text: Dull, unimaginative — nothing to do with walking. *Competent but* signals the blank must be a criticism, which eliminates *incisive*.

stem.text: The reasoning is ______: each step sounds plausible, but the second premise quietly assumes the conclusion.

explanation.text: Superficially plausible but false. *Tenuous* is the sophisticated distractor: tenuous reasoning looks weak, whereas specious reasoning looks strong, and "each step sounds plausible" demands the latter.

stem.text: The clerk was ______, correcting applicants' handwriting and lecturing them about paperwork no one had asked him about.

explanation.text: Meddlesome, offering unwanted help — not *official*. *Obliging* would be a compliment.

stem.text: Because the lease expired before the hearing, the question of who owed the repair costs became ______.

explanation.text: Here the "no longer relevant" sense, fixed by the expired lease. This word carries both senses, so only context settles it.

stem.text: The state ______ the land under an 1852 statute, compensating the owners at a rate they contested for decades.

explanation.text: Took for its own use. *Allocated* and *apportioned* mean distributing something you already hold, which the contested compensation shows is not the case.

stem.text: The authors ______ their claim considerably in the final section, noting that it may hold only for temperate climates.

explanation.text: To limit or narrow a claim, not to make it eligible. *Amplify* is the reverse and *substantiate* would add support rather than restrict scope.

stem.text: Residents complained of the ______ fumes drifting from the rendering plant, which made it unpleasant to sit outdoors.

explanation.text: Offensive-smelling. *Noisy* is the trap the word's spelling sets, and fumes from a rendering plant are a smell problem.

stem.text: The board voted to ______ the practice, permitting it explicitly for the first time after years of ambiguity.

explanation.text: Here the approving sense, fixed by "permitting it explicitly."

stem.text: Although the technique is now ______, it was regarded as reckless when first proposed: surgeons of the era refused outright to attempt it.

explanation.text: Two constraints: the contrast with "reckless" and the fact that it is still done today. *Obsolete* satisfies "now" but contradicts the contrast; *experimental* and *controversial* fail to contrast with reckless at all.

stem.text: The study's sample was large but ______: nearly all participants were recruited from a single university, so the findings may not extend to other populations.

explanation.text: The "but" demands a flaw, and the colon specifies which flaw: findings may not generalize. *Inadequate* satisfies "but" while contradicting "large," and *heterogeneous* contradicts the single-university detail.

stem.text: Far from being ______, the reforms were the product of two decades of quiet negotiation among people who mostly disliked one another.

explanation.text: "Far from being ___" inverts the blank, so it must be the opposite of twenty years of quiet negotiation. *Deliberate* and *protracted* are what the reforms actually were — right meaning, wrong slot.

stem.text: The author neither endorses the movement nor dismisses it; her stance throughout is ______.

explanation.text: Must fit both halves of "neither endorses nor dismisses." *Evasive* fits the absence of a position but adds an accusation of dodging that the sentence never makes.

stem.text: The instrument is not merely ______ but genuinely novel: no previous device measured this quantity at all.

explanation.text: "Not merely ___ but genuinely novel" requires a lesser version of the same positive quality. The other three are negatives, which the construction cannot accommodate.

stem.text: The committee voted to ______ the researcher, barring him from federal funding applications for five years.

explanation.text: The penalizing sense this time — the same word as Q145, decided entirely by "barring him from funding." If you answered both correctly, you are reading context rather than recalling a definition.

stem.text: The policy was both popular and ______: approval ratings stayed above 60 percent for a decade, and the deficit it was designed to close actually shrank.

explanation.text: Two facts are given: sustained popularity and a shrinking deficit. *Contentious* contradicts the first, *expensive* and *symbolic* are unsupported by either.

stem.text: Despite the ______ of the evidence — a single ambiguous photograph — the claim circulated widely for years.

explanation.text: "Despite" plus a single ambiguous photograph requires scarcity. *Abundance*, *clarity*, and *weight* all fit the "despite" structure grammatically and contradict the evidence described — the classic half-read error.
